title: Responding to opportunities
blurb: Choose and justify exploit, enhance, share or reject (or simply accept) for an opportunity, and see how each mirrors a threat response.
question: A housing association is building 40 homes. It orders its steel this month to lock in a supplier discount, hires an energy consultant to strengthen a grant bid, agrees with a neighbouring developer to build a shared access road and split the saving, and turns down a rooftop solar farm that would delay handover by six months. Which response is each of these?

teach.body: A risk is an uncertain event that, if it occurs, would affect the project's objectives. An OPPORTUNITY is a risk with a positive effect: an upside. In plain English, it is a good thing that might happen, and if nobody manages it, it usually slips away. The PMQ syllabus names four opportunity responses: exploit, enhance, share and reject. 'Accept' is also used, meaning take the opportunity if it arises without acting to pursue it.

children.label: Exploit
children.sub: act to make sure it happens

children.label: Share
children.sub: partner with a third party, split the gain

children.label: Reject
children.sub: decide deliberately not to pursue it

teach.caption: Accept: no action to pursue it, but take it if it comes along.

teach.h: Mirror images of the threat responses
head: Threat
Opportunity
Shared idea
teach.caption: Avoid makes a threat impossible; exploit makes an opportunity certain. Reduce shrinks a threat; enhance grows an opportunity.

teach.body: EXPLOIT: take action so the opportunity definitely happens, such as ordering steel now to secure the discount. ENHANCE: raise the probability or size of the benefit without guaranteeing it, such as a stronger grant bid. SHARE: bring in a third party better able to realise it and split the benefit, such as a joint venture or a gain-share contract. REJECT: decide, on purpose and on record, not to pursue it because the cost, risk or distraction outweighs the gain.

teach.h: Housing project: which response is this?

rows.label: Order steel this month to lock in the discount
Hire a consultant to strengthen the grant bid
Build a shared road with the neighbour, split savings

Take a surplus-stock discount if one is offered

teach.note: Ask: are we making it certain, making it likelier or bigger, partnering on it, declining it, or just waiting to see?

teach.h: Deciding what to do with an opportunity

steps.label: Fit?
steps.sub: Within scope, objectives and risk appetite?

steps.label: Respond
steps.sub: Exploit, enhance or share; or reject

steps.label: Own it
steps.sub: Named owner tracks it to closure

teach.body: Pursuing an opportunity costs money and effort and can bring secondary threats, such as scope creep or delay. That is why rejecting can be the right answer. In a linear project, taking an opportunity that changes scope, time or cost goes through change control against the baseline. In an iterative project, the opportunity becomes a backlog item the product owner can prioritise for the next time box, so short cycles make it quicker to seize an upside, such as releasing a popular feature early.

teach.text: Exam traps: EXPLOIT makes an opportunity certain; ENHANCE only improves the odds or the size. SHARE is for opportunities (both parties gain); TRANSFER is for threats. REJECT is a deliberate, recorded decision, not forgetting about it. And avoid or reduce are threat words: they are never the answer for an opportunity.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Explain that an opportunity is an uncertain event with a positive effect on objectives.
Name and define the response (e.g. enhance: increase probability or benefit).
Apply it with a concrete action from the scenario.
Justify it: benefit against cost, effort and any secondary threats, within scope and appetite.
Note who owns it and how it is tracked (change control or the backlog).
PMQ opportunity responses: exploit, enhance, share, reject. Accept means take it if it arises.
Exploit makes it certain; enhance improves probability or benefit.
Share brings in a partner and splits the gain; it mirrors transfer.
Reject is a deliberate decision when costs or risks outweigh the benefit.
Linear: change control. Iterative: the product owner prioritises it in the backlog.

summary: You can now choose exploit, enhance, share, reject or accept for any opportunity and justify the choice against cost, risk and fit. You can also pair each response with its threat mirror and explain how opportunities are taken up in linear and iterative projects.

A.q: A contractor will earn a £50,000 bonus if it finishes a month early. It moves its most experienced crew onto the job to make certain the early finish happens. Which response is this?
A.why: Committing resources to make sure the opportunity is realised is exploiting it: the aim is to remove the uncertainty.

whyNot.0: Enhance improves the odds without aiming to guarantee them; here the contractor is acting to make it certain.
whyNot.1: No third party is brought in to share the bonus.
whyNot.3: Accepting would mean waiting to see whether the early finish happens.

A.q: Which opportunity response involves working with a third party who is better able to realise the opportunity?
A.why: Share brings in a partner who is better placed to realise the opportunity, with the benefit split between them.

whyNot.1: Transfer is the threat response that passes financial impact to a third party.
whyNot.2: Exploit is done by the project itself to make the opportunity certain.
whyNot.3: Enhance is the project's own action to improve probability or benefit.

options: Act so that the opportunity is certain to happen
Raise its probability or the size of its benefit
Bring in a partner to realise it and split gains
Decide formally not to pursue the opportunity
A.why: Enhance increases the probability and/or the positive impact of an opportunity, without guaranteeing it.

whyNot.2: Partnering and splitting the gain is share.
whyNot.3: Deciding not to pursue it is reject.

B.q: A charity may win a lottery grant for its new community hub. It hires a professional bid writer to strengthen the application. Which response is this?
B.why: A stronger bid raises the probability of winning, but the outcome is still uncertain: that is enhancing the opportunity.

whyNot.0: Exploit would make the grant certain, which a bid writer cannot do.
whyNot.1: The charity is pursuing the opportunity, not declining it.
whyNot.2: The bid writer is paid for a service; they don't share the grant.

B.q: A retailer's IT project could add a loyalty feature, but doing so would delay a legally required go-live date. The sponsor decides not to pursue it and records why. Which response is this?
B.why: A deliberate, recorded decision not to pursue an opportunity, because the cost or risk outweighs the benefit, is rejecting it.

whyNot.0: Accept means taking the opportunity if it comes along; here it is actively turned down.
whyNot.1: Avoid is a threat response, not an opportunity response.
whyNot.3: Reduce is a threat response that lowers probability or impact.

B.q: Which pairing of a threat response with its opportunity 'mirror' is CORRECT?
B.why: Transfer (threats) and share (opportunities) both involve a third party.

whyNot.0: Avoid mirrors exploit: both remove the uncertainty.
whyNot.2: Reduce mirrors enhance: both change probability or impact.
whyNot.3: Accept mirrors reject or accept: no proactive action.

C.q: Two neighbouring developers both need a new access road. They agree to build it together and split the cost saving. What is the main reason this counts as SHARING an opportunity?
options: A third party helps realise it and shares the gain
The threat of high costs moves to the other firm
The road is now certain, so the gain is being exploited
No action is needed until the road is complete
C.why: Share means working with another party better placed to realise the opportunity, with the benefit divided between them.

whyNot.1: Moving the cost of a threat to another party would be transfer; here both parties gain.
whyNot.2: The agreement involves a partner and a split benefit, which is what makes it share rather than exploit.
whyNot.3: The developers are acting together, so this is not passive acceptance.

C.q: Which is NOT a sound reason to reject an opportunity?
options: It would breach a fixed regulatory deadline
Its cost and effort outweigh the likely benefit
It falls outside the organisation's risk appetite
The team didn't get round to analysing it
C.why: Rejection should be a deliberate decision based on analysis. Failing to analyse an opportunity is neglect, not a reason.

whyNot.0: Protecting a fixed regulatory deadline is a sound reason to decline an opportunity that threatens it.
whyNot.1: If pursuing it costs more than it returns, rejecting it is sensible.
whyNot.2: Opportunities outside the risk appetite can rightly be rejected.

C.q: A builder hears a supplier might offer a surplus-stock discount later in the year. It takes no action to pursue it, but will gladly take the discount if offered. Which response is this?
C.why: Taking an opportunity if it arises, without acting to make it more likely, is accepting it.

whyNot.0: Reject would mean deciding to decline the discount; the builder will take it.
whyNot.2: The builder is doing nothing to raise the chance of the discount.
whyNot.3: The builder is not acting to make the discount certain.

reteach.title: Think of planning a music festival
reteach.question: A small festival might get some lucky breaks this year. How would the organisers handle each one?

blocks.body: A famous band's tour passes nearby the same weekend. The organisers sign them today, before anyone else does: EXPLOIT. Local radio might feature the festival, so they send presenters free passes and a press pack: ENHANCE. A brewery offers to run the bars and split the profit: SHARE. A TV crew wants to film, but would need a stage rebuild the team has no time for: REJECT. A bigger crowd if the sun shines? They'll take it: ACCEPT.

head: Response
Festival action
rows: Say no to the TV crew

blocks.text: Sending the press pack doesn't guarantee the radio feature, so it is ENHANCE, not exploit. Signing the band locks it in, so that one is EXPLOIT.

explain.body: Act to make sure the opportunity happens, removing the uncertainty. Typical actions: commit your best people, buy or book early, lock in a deal. It mirrors avoid, which removes a threat's uncertainty.

items.label: before: the discount may be missed

test.q: What does EXPLOITING an opportunity aim to do?
options: Hand the opportunity to a partner
Wait to see if the opportunity comes
test.why: Exploit removes the uncertainty so the opportunity is definitely realised.

whyNot.1: Making it more likely, without certainty, is enhance.
whyNot.2: Bringing in a partner is share.

explain.body: Increase the probability that the opportunity occurs, or the size of its benefit, or both, without guaranteeing it. Typical actions: a stronger bid, extra marketing, meeting a funder's preferred criteria. It mirrors reduce.

explain.caption: Illustrative figures: better odds, but still not certain.

test.q: A museum might be chosen to host a touring exhibition, which would boost visitor income. It upgrades its gallery lighting to meet the tour's preferred standard. Which response is this?
test.why: Meeting the preferred standard raises the chance of being chosen, but the decision is still the tour's: that is enhance.

whyNot.0: No partner is brought in to share the income.
whyNot.1: The museum cannot make selection certain, so this is not exploit.
whyNot.3: The museum is actively pursuing the opportunity, not declining it.

explain.body: Bring in a third party who is better able to realise the opportunity and split the benefit with them. Typical forms: joint ventures, partnerships, gain-share or target-cost contracts. It mirrors transfer, but with an upside both parties want.

explain.h: Share brings two parties' strengths together

test.q: Which is the clearest example of SHARING an opportunity?
options: Insuring the whole site against fire and flood damage
A gain-share deal splitting savings with a builder
Ordering early to lock in a guaranteed discount
Adding evidence to a bid to improve its chances
test.why: A gain-share arrangement brings in a partner and splits the upside: that is sharing.

whyNot.0: Insurance passes the cost of a threat to a third party: transfer.
whyNot.2: Locking in a guaranteed discount makes it certain: exploit.
whyNot.3: Improving the chances of a bid is enhance.

explain.body: Reject: a deliberate, recorded decision not to pursue an opportunity because its cost, risk or distraction outweighs the benefit, or it is outside scope or appetite. Accept: no action to pursue it, but take it if it turns up.

children.edge: No: costs or risks too high
children.label: Reject

test.q: What distinguishes REJECTING an opportunity from simply ignoring it?
options: Rejection passes the opportunity to a partner
Rejection is only allowed for small opportunities
Rejection means the opportunity can no longer occur
Rejection is a deliberate decision that is recorded
test.why: Rejecting is a conscious, documented choice based on analysis, so it can be explained and revisited. Ignoring is neglect.

whyNot.0: Handing it to a partner is share.
whyNot.1: Opportunities of any size may be rejected if the costs or risks outweigh the benefit.
whyNot.2: Rejecting doesn't change whether the event happens; it just means the project won't pursue it.
